style="text;html=1;whiteSpace=wrap;align=left;verticalAlign=top;fontSize=16;fontColor=#222222;fontStyle=1;spacing=4;" value="How to read it — follow the numbers" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="30" width="900" x="40" y="940" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="2ooY1s4R5xRWJ7JQftpv-53" parent="1" style="rounded=1;arcSize=6;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fontSize=12;fillColor=#ffffff;strokeColor=#999999;strokeWidth=1.5;align=left;verticalAlign=middle;spacingLeft=8;spacingRight=8;spacingTop=2;spacingBottom=2;" value="<b>Write path (①–⑥)</b><br>① A service handles a request; the SDK emits spans without waiting.<br>② The local agent batches spans and sends them to the gateway.<br>③ The gateway checks them, then publishes to Kafka using trace_id as the key.<br>④ The same trace_id always lands on the same assembler instance.<br>⑤ The assembler gathers every span of that trace, then decides once the trace is done (or the wait time runs out).<br>⑥ Not interesting → DROP. Error / slow / priority → KEEP (⑦).<br><br><b>Why Kafka + assembler?</b> To guarantee errors are never lost by chance, we must see the whole trace before sampling. That makes the assembler stateful, so Kafka keeps spans durable and routes by trace_id." vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="300" width="930" x="40" y="980" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="2ooY1s4R5xRWJ7JQftpv-54" parent="1" style="rounded=1;arcSize=6;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fontSize=12;fillColor=#ffffff;strokeColor=#999999;strokeWidth=1.5;align=left;verticalAlign=middle;spacingLeft=8;spacingRight=8;spacingTop=2;spacingBottom=2;" value="<b>Store &amp; read (⑦–⑬)</b><br>⑦–⑧ Kept traces are saved to hot storage by a separate writer, so a slow DB never stalls sampling.<br>⑨–⑩ Engineers query by trace_id through the Query Service, never the DB directly.<br>⑪–⑬ Old traces move to cheap cold storage, then are deleted when retention ends.<br><br><b>Control plane (C / M)</b><br>C1–C2 Operators change sampling/retention through a reviewed, audited API into the Policy Store.<br>C3–C4 Assemblers and the tiering job get the policy pushed (they keep the last good policy if the store is down).<br>M1–M3 Agent heartbeats and buffer metrics feed monitoring, which triggers scale-out." vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="300" width="930" x="990" y="980" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </root> </mxGraphModel> </diagram> </mxfile>

div.div: How to read it — follow the numbers

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 912px; height: 1px; padding-top: 1122px; margin-left: 30px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div:
Write path (①–⑥)
① A service handles a request; the SDK emits spans without waiting.
② The local agent batches spans and sends them to the gateway.
③ The gateway checks them, then publishes to Kafka using trace_id as the key.
④ The same trace_id always lands on the same assembler instance.
⑤ The assembler gathers every span of that trace, then decides once the trace is done (or the wait time runs out).
⑥ Not interesting → DROP. Error / slow / priority → KEEP (⑦).
Why Kafka + assembler? To guarantee errors are never lost by chance, we must see the whole trace before sampling. That makes the assembler stateful, so Kafka keeps spans durable and routes by trace_id.

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 912px; height: 1px; padding-top: 1122px; margin-left: 980px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div:
Store & read (⑦–⑬)
⑦–⑧ Kept traces are saved to hot storage by a separate writer, so a slow DB never stalls sampling.
⑨–⑩ Engineers query by trace_id through the Query Service, never the DB directly.
⑪–⑬ Old traces move to cheap cold storage, then are deleted when retention ends.
Control plane (C / M)
C1–C2 Operators change sampling/retention through a reviewed, audited API into the Policy Store.
C3–C4 Assemblers and the tiering job get the policy pushed (they keep the last good policy if the store is down).
M1–M3 Agent heartbeats and buffer metrics feed monitoring, which triggers scale-out.
